items.title: 7.2.2 Measuring the rate of a chemical reaction

source_refs.note: Topic 7.2.2, printed pages 147-148 (Table 7.1 and Figure 7.2), as printed, with Quick Check 7.3.

blocks.text: The measurement of rate of a chemical reaction involves the determination of the concentration of reactants or products at regular time intervals as the reaction progresses.

blocks.caption: Table 7.1 Change in concentration of HI with regular intervals, 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g)

blocks.text: To determine the rate of reaction for a given length of time, a graph is plotted between time on x-axis and concentration of a reactant on y-axis, whereby a curve is obtained. To illustrate it, let us investigate the decomposition of HI to H₂ and I₂ at 500°C. By using the data, a graph is plotted as shown in Fig (7.3). The graph is between time on x-axis and concentration of HI in mol dm⁻³ on y-axis. Since HI is a reactant, so it is a falling curve. The steepness of the concentration-time curve reflects the progress of reaction. Greater the slope of curve near the start of reaction, greater is the rate of reaction.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The graph of these data is Figure 7.2 (below); Figure 7.3 is the colorimetry picture in 7.2.3.

In order to measure the rate of reaction, draw a tangent say, at 100 seconds, on the curve and measure the slope of that tangent. The slope of the tangent is the rate of reaction at that point i.e., after 100 seconds. A right-angled triangle ABC is completed with a tangent as hypotenuse. Figure 7.2 shows that in 100 sec, the change in concentration is 0.04 mol dm⁻³. The rate is then calculated by using the following expression.

blocks.text_alt: rate = 0.04 mol dm⁻³ / 100 sec = 4×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

blocks.text: This value of rate means that the concentration of HI is decreasing by 2.5 moles per dm⁻³ every second during the given interval.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Figure 7.2 the tangent falls by 0.04 mol dm⁻³ over about 160 s (the base CB of the triangle), not 100 s, so the rate at 100 s is 0.04 / 160 = about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (Table 7.1 gives a similar 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ around 100 s). The HI concentration is falling by about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³, not 2.5 moles per dm³, every second.

blocks.alt: Grid graph of [HI] (0 to 0.10 mol dm-3) against Time (s) (0 to 350). A green falling curve passes through yellow data points at 50 to 350 s, from 0.10 at the start. A blue tangent touches the curve at 100 s and runs from 0.08 at the y-axis to below 0.04. A right-angled triangle ABC: vertical leg from A at 0.08 down to C at 0.04 on the y-axis, labelled 0.04 mol dm-3, and horizontal leg from C to B on the tangent at about 164 s.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.2: The change in the HI concentration with time to the reaction 2HI(g) to H2(g) + I2(g) at 508 degrees C (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 7.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 7.2 labels the y-axis '[H1]' and puts the letter X on the vertical axis and Y on the horizontal one; the axis is [HI], with Y vertical and X horizontal, as drawn above.

If we plot a graph between time on x-axis and concentration of any of the products i.e H₂ or I₂, then a rising curve is obtained. The value of the tangent at 100 seconds will give the same value of rate of reaction as 4×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
book_errors: the same value of rate of reaction as 4×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In 2HI → H₂ + I₂, two moles of HI give one mole each of H₂ and I₂, so the tangent to the H₂ or I₂ curve at 100 s is half as steep as the HI tangent: about 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (half of 2.5 × 10⁻⁴), not the same value and not 4 × 10⁻⁴.

items: Plot the data in Table 7.1 for HI.
Calculate the rate after 300 sec (when the concentration is 0.03 mol dm⁻³) by drawing a tangent.
Use the same method to calculate the rate of reaction at HI concentrations of 0.10 mol dm⁻³, 0.050 mol dm⁻³ and 0.02 mol dm⁻³.
What do you deduce about the rate of the reaction with time from these calculations?
At which concentration, the rate is highest, and lowest?
